_meta.origin: Ninja Inkflow CE US and UK Spelling Database

entries.pattern_description: Verbs formed with the suffix -ize, and the nouns, adjectives and agent nouns derived from them.
entries.uk_rule: Most UK usage uses -ise, -ises, -ised, -ising, -isation. Oxford spelling, used by some UK publishers, keeps -ize.
entries.exceptions: Words that end in -ise in both varieties are not part of this pattern: advertise, advise, comprise, compromise, devise, disguise, exercise, improvise, revise, supervise, surprise. Words that end in -ize in both: capsize, prize, seize, size. Verbs ending -yze/-yse are a separate pattern (YZE_YSE).
entries.known_ambiguities: Whether a UK document uses -ise or Oxford -ize depends on house style. The en_GB-ise dictionary used for validation lists -ise only, so it cannot confirm -ize as an acceptable UK alternative.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Look up the exact form in the table. Never replace -ize with -ise by pattern. Read the document setting (en-GB or en-GB-oxendict). Skip words listed in Common_Spellings. Skip protected names such as World Health Organization.

entries.pattern_description: A small set of verbs ending in -yze (US) or -yse (UK).
entries.uk_rule: Use -yse, -yses, -ysed, -ysing in all UK usage, including Oxford spelling.
entries.exceptions: The related nouns ending in -ysis (analysis, paralysis, catalysis) are the same in both varieties.
entries.known_ambiguities: UK analyses is also the plural noun of analysis. A UK form found in a US document may therefore be the noun.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: In a UK document, flag the -yze form and correct it. In a US document, flag the -yse verb forms only after a part-of-speech check.

entries.pattern_description: Nouns that end in -or in US English and -our in UK English, with inflected and derived forms.
entries.uk_rule: Use -our (colour, honour, behaviour). Many derived words keep the u (colourful, favourite, honourable).
entries.exceptions: The pattern does not apply to words that end in -or in both varieties (actor, doctor, error, motor). Words ending -our in both: hour, flour, sour, devour. The UK drops the u before -ous, -ary, -ific and -ation, so these are the same in both varieties: humorous, vigorous, rigorous, honorary, honorific, coloration.
entries.known_ambiguities: Proper names and fixed phrases keep their own spelling (Labor Day, rigor mortis, Australian Labor Party). Glamour is the usual spelling in both varieties.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Use exact-form lookup only. Do not remove or add a u by rule. Check Protected_Terms before flagging.

entries.pattern_description: Words that end in -er in US English and -re in UK English.
entries.uk_rule: Use -re (centre, fibre, theatre, litre, metre).
entries.exceptions: Most -er words are the same in both varieties (number, member, paper). Instrument names ending -meter are the same (thermometer, barometer, speedometer).
entries.known_ambiguities: UK meter is a measuring device and metre is the unit, so meter is context-dependent. UK micrometre is the unit and micrometer the instrument. Some US venues and companies use the -re spelling in their names.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Treat centre/fibre/litre and the prefixed units as definite. Treat meter and micrometer as context-dependent. Protect venue and company names.

entries.pattern_description: Nouns that end in -og in US usage and -ogue in UK usage.
entries.us_rule: catalog is the usual US form. Analog is common in electronics. Dialog is common for computer dialogs.
entries.uk_rule: Use -ogue (catalogue, analogue, dialogue).
entries.exceptions: Other -ogue words are the same in both varieties (monologue, prologue, epilogue, rogue).
entries.known_ambiguities: US English also accepts dialogue and analogue. In computing, UK writers often use dialog and analog.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: catalog/catalogue is definite. Treat dialog and analog as context-dependent.

entries.pattern_description: Words that end in -se in US English and -ce in UK English, plus the UK noun/verb split practise/practice.
entries.us_rule: defense, offense, pretense. License and practice are used for noun and verb.
entries.uk_rule: defence, offence, pretence. UK uses licence (noun) and license (verb), and practice (noun) and practise (verb).
entries.exceptions: Derived adjectives are the same in both varieties (offensive, defensive). Licensed, licensing and licensee are the same. Practice as a noun is the same in both.
entries.known_ambiguities: License and practice cannot be corrected without knowing the part of speech.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: defence, offence and pretence are definite. Flag license/licence and practice/practise for a context check only.

entries.pattern_description: Differences in whether a final consonant is doubled before a suffix, or whether the word ends in -ll or -l.
entries.us_rule: Final l is doubled only when the last syllable is stressed (traveled, canceled, labeled, modeler). Words such as enroll, fulfill and skillful keep ll.
entries.uk_rule: The final l is doubled in most cases (travelled, cancelled, labelled). Words such as enrol, fulfil and skilful have a single l.
entries.exceptions: Past and -ing forms of fulfil, enrol, distil and instil double the l in both varieties (fulfilled, enrolling). Words with a stressed last syllable double the consonant in both (compelled, controlled, patrolled).
entries.known_ambiguities: Some UK double-l forms also appear in US writing. The dictionary columns in the table record this.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Use exact-form lookup. Never add or remove an l by rule.

entries.pattern_description: Greek and Latin words, mostly medical, that keep ae or oe in UK English and use e in US English.
entries.us_rule: Use e (anemia, esophagus, fetus, pediatric, hemoglobin).
entries.uk_rule: Use ae or oe (anaemia, oesophagus, foetus, paediatric, haemoglobin).
entries.exceptions: Aesthetic and medieval are the same in both varieties. Some words keep ae in both.
entries.known_ambiguities: The en_GB-ise word list itself accepts some of the e forms (for example fetus), so UK practice is mixed. Those records are marked disputed.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Flag as a suggestion. Do not autocorrect records marked needs_review or disputed. Follow the customer’s style sheet for medical terms.

entries.pattern_description: Chemical and medical words built on sulfur.
entries.uk_rule: Older UK usage uses sulph- (sulphur, sulphate).
entries.exceptions: None.
entries.known_ambiguities: IUPAC and many UK scientific publishers use sulf-, so the US form is not an error in UK scientific writing.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Treat the US form in a UK document as a style preference. Never autocorrect. Follow house style.

entries.pattern_description: Two element names that differ between varieties.
entries.uk_rule: aluminium, caesium
entries.exceptions: All other element names are the same in both varieties (sodium, platinum, helium).
entries.known_ambiguities: IUPAC names are aluminium and caesium, which US science writing may also use.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: aluminum is definite in a UK document. Check house style for US scientific text.

entries.pattern_description: Words in which UK English keeps the e after dg.
entries.uk_rule: judgement, acknowledgement, abridgement
entries.exceptions: None.
entries.known_ambiguities: UK legal writing uses judgment for a court’s decision.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Treat judgment/judgement and judgments/judgements as context-dependent. Other pairs are definite.

entries.pattern_description: Words in which UK English keeps a silent e before -ing or -able.
entries.uk_rule: ageing, likeable, sizeable
entries.exceptions: None.
entries.known_ambiguities: Both forms are common in UK writing for some words.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Use the dictionary column to decide whether the form is a mismatch or an accepted alternative.

entries.pattern_description: A few words spelled with k in US English and c in UK English.
entries.uk_rule: sceptic, mollusc, leucocyte
entries.exceptions: Leukaemia keeps the k in both varieties.
entries.known_ambiguities: UK medical writing often uses leukocyte.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Treat leukocyte as disputed. Other pairs are definite.

entries.pattern_description: Words in which UK English has ou.
entries.uk_rule: mould, smoulder, plough, moustache, moult
entries.exceptions: None.
entries.known_ambiguities: Mold and plow may be part of a fixed name or code.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Flag as definite. Check Protected_Terms first.

entries.pattern_description: Individual words that differ in a vowel or consonant.
entries.us_rule: gray, cozy, pajamas, tire, yogurt, chili
entries.uk_rule: grey, cosy, pyjamas, tyre, yoghurt, chilli
entries.exceptions: The SI unit gray (Gy) and proper names keep gray in UK text.
entries.known_ambiguities: Tire (to grow weary) is the same in both varieties.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Treat gray/grey and tire/tyre as context-dependent. Others are definite where the dictionary confirms them.

entries.pattern_description: Words with a different spelling in the two varieties that fit no pattern above.
entries.us_rule: program, airplane, check, curb, story, ton, disk, inquiry
entries.uk_rule: programme, aeroplane, cheque, kerb, storey, tonne, disc, enquiry
entries.exceptions: Computer program is the same in both varieties. Check (to verify), curb (to restrain) and story (a narrative) are the same.
entries.known_ambiguities: The UK form has a narrower meaning than the US form.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Treat most as context-dependent. Never autocorrect.

entries.pattern_description: Verbs whose past form can end in -ed or -t.
entries.uk_rule: learnt, dreamt, burnt are accepted alongside the -ed forms
entries.exceptions: None.
entries.known_ambiguities: Both forms are accepted in UK English.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Treat as an accepted alternative. Report only at info level.

entries.pattern_name: Words with more than one accepted spelling
entries.pattern_description: Words for which a variety accepts two spellings (not a US against UK difference).
entries.uk_rule: See uk_alternatives.
entries.exceptions: None.
entries.known_ambiguities: Dictionaries differ on which form is preferred.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Accept the recorded alternatives. Flag only when one document uses two forms of the same word.

entries.pattern_name: Words where dictionaries or style guides differ
entries.pattern_description: Records marked disputed, where the word list accepts the form of the other variety or style guides disagree.
entries.uk_rule: Varies.
entries.exceptions: None.
entries.known_ambiguities: No single authority has been consulted. House style decides.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Report at info level as a style preference. Never autocorrect. Allow a customer override.

entries.pattern_name: Same spelling, different regional meaning or usage
entries.pattern_description: Words spelled the same in both varieties whose meaning differs by region.
entries.uk_rule: See Common_Spellings regional_usage_notes.
entries.exceptions: None.
entries.known_ambiguities: The correct sense depends on the sentence and the audience.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Never change automatically. Show the note to the editor when the document variant is known.

entries.pattern_name: Proper nouns, trademarks and organisation names
entries.pattern_description: Names that keep their own spelling in any document.
entries.us_rule: Official names, for example Department of Defense.
entries.uk_rule: Official names, for example Ministry of Defence.
entries.examples: World Health Organization; Labour Party; Center Parcs
entries.exceptions: None.
entries.known_ambiguities: A name may appear in a form that is not its official spelling.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Mask the exact, case-sensitive phrases in Protected_Terms before any lookup. Add article-specific names from the document.

entries.pattern_name: Spelling that depends on grammar or derivation
entries.pattern_description: Cases in which the correct spelling depends on part of speech or on the derived word.
entries.us_rule: practice (noun and verb); license (noun and verb)
entries.uk_rule: practice (noun), practise (verb); licence (noun), license (verb)
entries.exceptions: Derived words may lose the u (honorary) or keep it (honourable).
entries.known_ambiguities: A single surface form can be correct as one word and wrong as another.
entries.recommended_validation_behavior: Do not use blanket rules. Send flagged forms to the context-sensitive layer, or leave them as flag-only.
